title: Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: CUDA 13.4 adds transparent per-workload GPU memory enforcement, and NVIDIA released an open-source GPU Fractioning Operator plus KAI Scheduler v0.18.0 NvFractions mode so Kubernetes clusters can run fractional-GPU workloads with guaranteed and burstable memory and a choice of time-slicing or SM-sharing. The practical aim is higher GPU utilization on existing infrastructure.

insights.claim: Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU, so allocating whole devices leaves capacity idle, while sharing lets platform teams serve more workloads on infrastructure they already own.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: GPU utilization efficiency is a direct lever on AI infrastructure return on capital, and a headwind to raw GPU unit demand if sharing becomes widespread.
insights.quote: Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU.

insights.claim: CUDA 13.4 enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application, so an allocation above the requested size fails just as it would on a smaller GPU.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Hard memory limits without MIG hardware partitioning make multi-tenant GPU sharing safer on more GPU types.
insights.quote: An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU.
insights.locator: Here is what the CUDA release brings

insights.claim: Workloads can request a guaranteed minimum plus a burstable maximum of GPU memory, and each sees only a fraction of the total memory.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Burstable memory lets operators overcommit more safely, raising effective utilization.
insights.locator: Here is what the CUDA release brings

insights.claim: The existing NVIDIA sharing options differ in isolation: MIG gives hardware-isolated instances, time-slicing lets processes take turns without memory enforcement, and MPS lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Choosing the right sharing mode is a trade-off between isolation, flexibility and utilization.

insights.claim: CUDA cannot be used by Kubernetes alone; each GPU node must supervise the required daemons, apply per-container memory limits and compute mode before the process starts, and report usage per fraction rather than per whole GPU.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: A node-level operator is the missing glue that turns a CUDA feature into usable cluster capability.
insights.quote: The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes
insights.locator: The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes

insights.claim: The new open-source gpu-fractioning Kubernetes operator is hosted under the KAI Scheduler GitHub organization, runs next to the NVIDIA GPU Operator, sets up MPS on every GPU node, applies memory limits and compute modes and measures use per fraction.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Shipping this as open source under the KAI organization encourages ecosystem adoption and keeps NVIDIA's stack the default control plane.
insights.locator: GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator

insights.claim: The operator is scheduler-agnostic: any Kubernetes scheduler that writes the documented per-container Pod annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA, leaving the scheduler to choose GPUs with free memory and avoid mixing compute modes.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: An annotation-based contract lowers the barrier for other schedulers to integrate, which could widen the standard.
insights.quote: Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA.
insights.locator: How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler v0.18.0 is the first scheduler integrated with gpu-fractioning, via its NvFractions GPU-sharing mode that is enabled with a Helm flag and also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: NVIDIA-owned scheduling software is the reference implementation, tying the Run:ai lineage to CUDA features.
insights.locator: Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler

insights.claim: Workloads can declare a guaranteed request and an optional limit by absolute memory size or by GPU portion; if the limit is omitted the workload is capped at exactly its request, and a portion limit must exceed the gpu-fraction and be less than 1.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Explicit burst semantics make capacity planning and chargeback for shared GPUs more tractable.
insights.quote: The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for.
insights.locator: How far it may grow: The limit

insights.claim: A request applies per device, so a 40Gi request across four devices yields 40Gi on each of four GPUs via the gpu-fraction-num-devices annotation.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Fractional sharing extends to multi-GPU inference, not only single-GPU jobs.
insights.quote: A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs.

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler never places time-slicing and SM-sharing workloads on the same GPU and tracks the mode per GPU, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Per-GPU mode tracking keeps scheduling flexible without mixing incompatible isolation models.

insights.claim: Time-slicing is serial with each workload in its own error domain, giving full error isolation, while SM-sharing runs workloads in parallel across streaming multiprocessors but in a single shared error domain.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Choose time-slicing for untrusted or batch jobs and SM-sharing only for workloads that can be trusted to run together.
insights.quote: In this mode, workloads share a single error domain.
insights.locator: How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing

insights.claim: With SM-sharing the GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs dynamically, so splits settle near 1/n when all are busy and a single active workload can use all SMs when neighbors are idle.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Dynamic SM allocation improves utilization for bursty inference traffic compared with static partitions.
insights.quote: Nothing is carved out in advance.
insights.locator: How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing

insights.claim: The suggested uses are SM-sharing for trusted inference servers that should run concurrently, and time-slicing as the default for development or batch work such as notebooks and small fine-tuning runs.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Matches sharing mode to workload type, a practical rule of thumb for cluster operators.
insights.locator: Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning
